posts.reason: Turns the 1983 Ironies of Automation into working rules for agentic coding, such as a vibe limit per change and treating repeated "yes, continue" as a warning sign.
Five agent-built runs per framework with medians and ranges for cost, tokens, bytes and Lighthouse, plus thread pushback on whether a content-site benchmark says anything about interactive apps.
A rare first-party account of replacing a widely used standard-library API: which v1 behaviours were flaws, what the new options fix, and how v1 and v2 stay compatible during migration.

Explains how the browser will auto-darken light pages, how text, SVG and images are transformed, and the one CSS declaration sites use to opt out, with a thread on whether color-scheme was designed well.
A footnoted essay using Barcelona, Riga and Nancy to argue that Art Nouveau was too bespoke to scale, and that classicism and then modernism won by being repeatable.

Traces an OpenSSH bypass through commits from 1980 to 2026 to a sentinel return value colliding with disabled accounts, and the thread turns that into an argument about null returns versus option types.
A year's update across coding, research, writing and art, each section ending in a verdict table, from someone running five or six agents but still writing their own prose.
Applies the same 1983 automation paper to incident response, citing an endoscopy detection drop and FAA manual-flying rules; note it ends in a vendor pitch.
Perf counters show half a naive GROUP BY's CPU slots waiting on DRAM, and radix partitioning into cache-sized tables cuts both, with code for both versions.
Makes the case for a git-style history of the US Code, reproducing 361 of 365 amendments and citing studies of LLMs applying superseded statutes.
A decade of reverse engineering DOS Wing Commander, from memory maps and trampolines to a WebRTC browser port with co-op via a room code.
